title: Trust in pardon already obtained is not the formal act of justifying faith; hope of mercy is required
source_text: XXXVIII. Nec etiam inter Scholam Romanam & Reformatam controversia est, An certa fiducia de impetrata a Deo peccatorum venia sit proprius, formalis, & specificus actus fidei justificantis, ratione cujus in Scriptura dicimur fide justificari. Neque enim id communiter asserunt Protestantes. Referunt quidem illi in peccatore poenitente & justificando, fiduciam de obtinenda peccatorum remissione a Dei per Christum misericordia, tanquam conditionem necessariam & praeviam ad justificationem, minime vero fiduciam de remissione illa jam impetrata. Sicut autem Protestantes ultro fatentur fiduciam de jam impetrata remissione peccatorum non esse illud per quod justificatur impius, sive aliquid ad ejus justificationem praevium: ita quoque Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non negant ad hoc ut aliquis a peccato justificetur, necessariam esse in eo spem veniae, & fiduciam de obtinenda a Deo misericordia. Imo res est quam sanxit & definivit ipsa Tridentina Synodus, Sess. 6. cap. 6. Ubi inter alia docet homines ad justificationem disponi, Dum peccatores se esse intelligentes, a divina justitia timore, quo utiliter concutiuntur, ad considerandam Dei misericordiam se convertendo, in spem eriguntur, fidentes Deum sibi propter Christum propitium fore. Quod probat ex illo Christi dicto ad paralyticum, Confide fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua. Marc. 2.
pass_a_gloss: Nor also is there controversy between the Roman and Reformed School whether a certain trust concerning pardon of sins obtained from God is the proper, formal, and specific act of justifying faith, by reason of which in Scripture we are said to be justified by faith. For Protestants do not commonly assert that. They do indeed refer in the penitent sinner to be justified a trust concerning obtaining remission of sins from God’s mercy through Christ, as a necessary and prior condition for justification, but by no means a trust concerning that remission already obtained. And just as Protestants freely confess that trust concerning remission of sins already obtained is not that by which the ungodly is justified, or something prior to his justification: so also the doctors of the Roman Church do not deny that for someone to be justified from sin there is necessary in him hope of pardon and trust concerning obtaining mercy from God. Nay, it is a matter which the Tridentine Synod itself sanctioned and defined, Sess. 6. cap. 6. Where among other things it teaches that men are disposed to justification when, understanding themselves to be sinners, by fear of divine justice by which they are usefully shaken, turning themselves to consider God’s mercy, they are raised into hope, trusting that God will be propitious to them for Christ’s sake. Which it proves from that saying of Christ to the paralytic, Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven you. Mark 2.
pass_b_english: Justifying faith’s prior act is refuge-trust toward mercy, not assurance of pardon already sealed.
Trent itself requires hope of pardon in the disposing sinner—common ground Le Blanc presses.
